name: Aeternum-Glacies
specific_features: Crystalline ice caves with acoustic properties
description: Aeternum-Glacies is a world frozen in eternal winter, its surface locked beneath ice sheets that reach depths of forty kilometers in places, burying whatever geological history the planet once possessed beneath a crystalline tomb. The ice is not uniform but layered in strata of different compositions, each layer recording a different epoch of the planet's atmospheric chemistry like rings in a tree. Cryovolcanic geysers erupt periodically along tectonic ridges, spraying plumes of liquid water and ammonia crystals that freeze into glittering columns before they touch the ground.

The thin atmosphere scatters what little starlight reaches this distant world into perpetual twilight shades of blue and violet, while the planet's strong magnetic field generates aurora displays that span from horizon to horizon in curtains of green and crimson. Sound travels strangely across the ice plains, whispers carrying for kilometers in the cold dense air near the surface while the crystalline caves beneath produce haunting harmonic resonances when wind passes through their openings. The cold is absolute and patient, the kind that finds every gap in insulation and punishes every moment of carelessness.

Beneath the ice, a liquid ocean persists, heated by tidal forces from the gas giant this world orbits. Probe missions have confirmed microbial life in this subsurface sea, chemotrophic organisms clustering around hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor in communities that have evolved in complete isolation for billions of years. The discovery confirmed that life can persist in environments once considered impossibly hostile, and the unique biochemistry of these organisms has attracted intense scientific interest.

Establishing research stations on Aeternum-Glacies requires drilling through kilometers of ice to reach the subsurface ocean, a process that takes months and risks contaminating the pristine ecosystem below. Three permanent stations currently operate, each maintaining boreholes through which submersible probes explore the dark waters. The ice itself has commercial value as an ultra-pure water source, but environmental protections limit extraction to surface layers only. The deeper question remains whether the subsurface ocean harbors more complex life in regions the probes have not yet reached, as sonar readings occasionally return echoes that match no known geological formation.
